questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the framing work an epigraph performs on a file
questions.stem: One file note opens with a line about a door that cannot be locked once it has been opened. What does this epigraph do?

options.text: It states a principle the rest of the file will test, and its paradox frames the whole matter
It names the building where the dispute arose, for the reader's orientation
options.misconception: reads the epigraph as a factual location note

options.text: It proves the clerk copied the case heading from an earlier file
options.misconception: infers template reuse from the opening line

options.text: It shows the file has been reopened, since the door refers to a second reading
options.misconception: reads the image as evidence about the file's history

questions.explanation: An epigraph frames the matter before the argument starts, and this paradox offers the principle the file will test. Reading it as a location or a copied heading misses that framing.
questions.hint: Consider what the opening line asks the file to examine.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a title and a closing image rhyme to complete a file
questions.stem: A file is titled 'The Matter of the Second Door', and the final note returns to a door, held open. Why does the title and the closing image rhyme like that?

answer.exemplar: The title promises an inquiry into a specific second opening, and the closing note shows a door deliberately held open rather than shut, so the image that named the file also closes it. That rhyme turns the case into a question about what happens when access cannot be withdrawn once it has been granted.

questions.explanation: The title's image and the closing image rhyme, so the file closes by returning to the terms it opened with. That rhyme frames the case as a question about access and its consequences.
questions.hint: Consider how the closing note answers the title.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a change of grammatical posture shifts a file's force
questions.stem: A clerk writes 'we submit that the position is untenable' and, two lines later, 'you have not addressed the letter of March'. Why does the note shift its grammatical posture?

answer.exemplar: The first sentence speaks in the collective voice of the instructing party, asserting a position the firm holds, while the second turns to address the recipient directly and accuses them of silence. The movement from 'we' to 'you' shifts the note from argument to reproach, and the firmness of the address is the point.

questions.explanation: Moving from 'we submit' to 'you have not addressed' turns a position into a direct accusation. The shift in grammatical posture carries the change from argument to reproach.
questions.hint: Consider what changes when the pronoun changes.

questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a closing note can confirm a title's claim
questions.stem: A file titled 'Twice Over' ends with a note that the same document was 'produced twice over, on the same morning'. Which judgement is best supported?

options.text: The ending contradicts the title, since the repetition was an accident rather than a theme
options.misconception: reads the ending as a contradiction of the title

options.text: The ending confirms the title by turning repetition into the file's central fact
The title refers to the hearing being listed twice in the court diary
options.misconception: infers a diary practice from the title

options.text: The ending shows the clerk suspects the other side has been careless with its papers
options.misconception: reads the note as an accusation of carelessness

questions.explanation: The closing confirms the title by making repetition the substance of the file, so shape and content agree. Reading it as contradiction, a diary practice or suspicion misses that agreement.
questions.hint: Consider what the title promised and what the note delivers.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a single closing word can complete a motif

stimulus.body: Exhibit 3 is a photograph of a hand resting on a table, taken from above, and nothing of the table is visible but the hand. The clerk refers to the hand in every note about that exhibit, and the final note adds only the word 'again'.

questions.stem: What does the clerk's final word accomplish?

options.text: It shows that the clerk has forgotten which exhibits have already been described
options.misconception: reads the single word as carelessness

options.text: It proves the photograph was presented to the court more than once
options.misconception: treats the word as evidence about presentation

options.text: It closes the file on the recurring image and asks the reader to see the hand once more
It signals that the clerk expects the party to produce a further photograph
options.misconception: infers a future request from the word

questions.explanation: The single word returns the reader to the hand that has run through the file, so the motif closes it. Reading it as carelessness, evidence of presentation or a request misses that.
questions.hint: Consider what the reader is being asked to picture.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise the mood a closing image creates for a file
questions.stem: A closing note describes the corridor as 'long, and lit by a single bulb at the far end'. Which judgement is best supported?

options.text: The description proves the clerk wanted the corridor photographed before it was altered
options.misconception: infers an evidential intention from a description

options.text: The detail is a plain record of the lighting, and nothing more need be read into it
options.misconception: insists the description carries no suggestion

options.text: The corridor and its bulb are being used to suggest that the case was neglected
options.misconception: reads the image as an allegation about neglect

options.text: The image sets the case at a distance the reader can approach but never quite reach

questions.explanation: A long corridor lit only at its far end gives the case a shape the reader can look down but never enter. Reading it as an evidential intention or an allegation of neglect misses that effect.
questions.hint: Consider the position the reader is left in by the image.
